overlap.title: What was the ephod Gideon made of the gold, and what did Israel do when it “went thither a whoring after it”?
overlap.summary: Gideon asks for the golden earrings of the spoil, makes “an ephod thereof” and puts it in his city, and all Israel goes “a whoring after it”. In the other verses compared an ephod is a thing a priest wears or brings. The passage does not say what Gideon’s ephod was, what it was for, or what the people did with it.
overlap.reasoning: In the verses compared outside Judges an ephod is listed among garments, is worn (“girded with a linen ephod”), or is brought by a priest when David wants to enquire. Gideon’s is made from the collected gold earrings, whose total weight is given as seventeen hundred shekels; the amount used in the ephod is not specified. It is “put” in a town, and draws “all Israel”. The passage gives the result, a snare to Gideon and his house, without saying what the object was or what the people did. That bears on what Gideon is being charged with, straight after he has said “the Lord shall rule over you”: making an idol, or setting up a means of enquiry or of priestly service away from the sanctuary.
overlap.scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the passage states: that it was a priestly garment heavy with gold, kept at Ophrah and used to enquire of God; that it was an image, or the covering of an image, which the people worshipped; that it was a trophy of the victory that came to be treated as holy. Limits: the phrase “went a whoring after” is used six verses later of the Baalim, which shows the phrase can be used of other gods and does not show what was done at Ophrah; Micah’s ephod at Judges 17:5 stands beside teraphim in “an house of gods” and Hosea 3:4 lists an ephod with an image and teraphim, but being named together does not make the things alike; the weight given is that of the earrings asked for, and the verse does not say that all of it went into the ephod. Brenton’s Greek keeps the Hebrew word as a name at Judges 8:27 and has a Greek word for a shoulder-piece at Exodus 28:6; that is a difference within the Greek edition and settles nothing about the object. Check made: a whole-word search of the packaged KJV of Judges for “ephod” finds 8:27, 17:5, 18:14, 18:17, 18:18 and 18:20; the other verses quoted were chosen from a search of 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel and Hosea for the same word. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible. These checked verses do not explicitly settle what Gideon’s ephod was. No H or G is proposed. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

overlap.title: “I have seen God face to face” and “no man hath seen God at any time”
overlap.summary: Jacob says he has seen God face to face and lived. Exodus says no man shall see God and live, and John says no man has seen God at any time.
overlap.reasoning: Jacob’s words are a plain claim to have seen God and survived. Exodus 33:20 says that cannot be, and John 1:18 says it has never happened. The KJV matches the Hebrew in Genesis and Exodus, and Brenton’s Greek has the same sense in both.
overlap.scope: No tag is proposed. The statement in Genesis is Jacob’s own; the narrator calls his opponent “a man” (32:24), and Hosea 12:4 says “the angel”. The verses can be reconciled if what Jacob saw was a man or an angel in whom he recognised God, and not God as Exodus and John mean it; Genesis 32 does not say so. Exodus 33:11 and 24:10, which bear on the same question inside Exodus, are not treated in this record; it adds only Jacob’s statement in Genesis. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.

studies.title: Can God be seen?
studies.summary: Exodus describes Moses speaking with God “face to face”; John says no one has seen God. The tension depends on whether “face to face” means literal sight.

studies.title: Judas and the field of blood
studies.summary: Matthew and Acts give different accounts of Judas's death and the field purchase.

studies.title: Water or ground: the animals’ origin
studies.summary: Genesis 1 can sound like birds came from water, while Genesis 2 says ground. The apparent conflict depends on how Genesis 1:20 is translated.

studies.title: Plants before people—or after?
studies.summary: Genesis 1 places vegetation before people; Genesis 2 describes no field plants before a cultivator. Whether this conflicts depends on which plants are meant.

studies.title: David’s census: two different totals
studies.summary: The census totals differ: Israel is 800,000 versus 1.1 million; Judah is 500,000 versus 470,000. Different counting rules are proposed but not established here.

studies.title: Herod, Quirinius, and the birth chronology
studies.summary: Matthew places Jesus’s birth under Herod; Luke links it to Quirinius’s census. The historical chronology creates a tension if the same census is intended.
